claims.text: Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 forms Cr–V-rich precipitates at about 8 dpa.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits low irradiation-induced hardening.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 has acceptable radiation resistance.
Approximately 4–5 at.% Hf can be substituted for an equal portion of Cr in nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 during bulk fabrication.
Adding approximately 4–5 at.% Hf in place of Cr will suppress Cr–V-rich precipitate formation through approximately 8 dpa.
The Hf-modified alloy will preserve the low hardening of the unmodified alloy.
The Hf-modified alloy will preserve radiation resistance.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain practical bulk manufacturability.
Irradiation between 350°C and 500°C is representative of fusion first-wall or divertor service conditions.
Hf atoms will preferentially segregate to grain boundaries and irradiation-induced defect sites.
Hf segregation will alter local chemistry and reduce Cr and V clustering.
Hf will modify local diffusion kinetics and act as a sink for vacancies and other defect species.
The effects of Hf on diffusion and defects will lower the thermodynamic driving force for Cr–V precipitate nucleation.
Hf will inhibit Cr–V precipitate growth without compromising beneficial dislocation-sink behavior.
After irradiation, the Hf-modified alloy will have fewer or no Cr–V-rich precipitates relative to the unmodified alloy.
After irradiation, the Hf-modified alloy will have hardness similar to that of the unmodified alloy.
The proposed benefits are limited to doses up to approximately 8 dpa and specimen temperatures from 350°C to 500°C.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome says that the Hf-modified alloy should have hardness similar to the baseline, whereas the falsification rule says that mechanical hardening comparable to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
